sections.h: Hired to curse, made to bless
sections.b: Balak king of Moab sends twice to Balaam son of Beor at Pethor by the Euphrates, offering great honor if he will curse Israel (Numbers 22:5–17). God first forbids him, then lets him go on one condition: he may speak only God's word. On the road his donkey sees the angel of the LORD three times, and God opens her mouth (22:22–35). From three heights Balak has altars built, and each time Balaam blesses instead (23:7–24:9). Unasked, he then foresees a star and scepter from Israel (24:15–19) and the fall of Moab, Edom, Amalek and Asshur.

A plaster wall text found in 1967 at Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley, from about 800 BC, begins "the book of Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods." The gods come to him at night, and he weeps over a coming disaster. It shows that Balaam was a famous seer in the region, honored by a people who were not Israelite.

Numbers 22–24 shows him refusing silver and gold and speaking true words, and Micah 6:5 recalls him as God's instrument. But Numbers 31:8, 16 says he advised the seduction at Peor and was killed among the Midianites, and Deuteronomy 23:4–5, Joshua 13:22 and Nehemiah 13:2 remember him as a hired curser. The New Testament (2 Peter 2:15–16; Jude 11; Revelation 2:14) and the rabbis (Mishnah Avot 5:19; Sanhedrin 10:2) follow the darker picture.
sections.refs: Numbers 31:8; Numbers 31:16; Deuteronomy 23:4–5; Joshua 13:22; Micah 6:5; 2 Peter 2:15–16; Revelation 2:14

common: Balaam was a greedy false prophet who wanted to curse Israel but could not.
uncommon: Some scholars think the Numbers 22–24 story admires Balaam as a foreigner who obeyed God, and that his bad reputation came from a separate tradition in chapter 31.

sections.b: When Israel worshiped the Baal of Peor and a plague broke out, Phinehas son of Eleazar killed the Simeonite leader Zimri and the Midianite princess Cozbi together, and the plague stopped (Numbers 25:6–9). God said Phinehas "was zealous with my zeal" and gave him "my covenant: peace," a lasting priesthood for his line (25:10–13). He goes with the army against Midian (31:6), leads the inquiry about the eastern altar (Joshua 22:13–34), and serves as high priest at Bethel (Judges 20:28).

Psalm 106:30–31 says his act "was reckoned to him as righteousness," and Ben Sira ranks him after Moses and Aaron (Sirach 45:23–24). Mattathias began the Maccabean revolt "as Phinehas did" (1 Maccabees 2:26), and the Zealots of the first century took him as their model. The rabbis praised him but fenced the precedent: zealots may act only in the moment, and a court would not tell them to (Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6; Bavli Sanhedrin 82a). Jewish tradition also identified him with Elijah, another priest-prophet "zealous for the LORD."
sections.refs: Psalm 106:28–31; Sirach 45:23–24; 1 Maccabees 2:26; 1 Maccabees 2:54; 1 Kings 19:10; Malachi 2:4–6

common: Phinehas is the model of zeal for God's honor.
uncommon: Some modern scholars read the Phinehas story mainly as a claim for the priestly line of Zadok, written to support its right to the high priesthood.

sections.b: Midian's elders join Moab in sending for Balaam (Numbers 22:4, 7). At Peor a Midianite chief's daughter, Cozbi, is killed with Zimri (25:6–15), and God tells Israel to treat Midian as an enemy because "they treated you as enemies with their tricks" (25:17–18). In chapter 31 twelve thousand Israelites kill Midian's five kings and Balaam, and Moses orders the boys and the women who were not virgins killed. Yet Moses' wife and father-in-law were Midianite (10:29–32; Exodus 2:21), and Midian is a strong nation again in Judges 6–8.

uncommon: Some scholars connect the Midianites with the copper mines and tent shrine at Timna and suggest Israel's God was first worshiped in Midian (the "Kenite" or "Midianite" hypothesis).

sections.b: Zelophehad of the tribe of Manasseh died in the wilderness with no sons. His five daughters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, stood before Moses, Eleazar and the whole assembly and asked for their father's land, so that his name would not be lost (Numbers 27:1–4). God answered, "Zelophehad's daughters have spoken rightly," and set a law for all Israel: sons inherit first, then daughters, then brothers, uncles and the nearest kin (27:7–11). In Numbers 36 their kinsmen worried that the land would pass to another tribe if they married outside it, and the ruling was added that heiresses marry within the father's tribe. The sisters married their cousins and kept the land (36:10–12), and Joshua gave it to them (Joshua 17:3–6).

The rabbis praised the sisters as "wise, interpreters of Scripture, and righteous" (Bavli Bava Batra 119b). Many modern readers see the case as a real advance for women's property rights in its world, with God siding with them against custom. Others, including many feminist scholars, note its limits: daughters inherit only without brothers, wives do not inherit, and Numbers 36 restricts whom heiresses may marry, so the law mainly protects the father's line. Job 42:15, where Job gives his daughters an inheritance among their brothers, goes further.

common: The daughters of Zelophehad won women the right to inherit land in Israel.
uncommon: Several sisters' names (Tirzah, Hoglah, Noah) are also place names in Manasseh's territory, and some scholars read the story as explaining how those districts became part of the tribe.

claude.title: The daughters as the anti-spies
claude.body: The spies made Israel's hearts turn away from the land (Numbers 32:9); these daughters go to court to get a share of it. Numbers seems to frame its new generation with their story (27; 36) as the opposite of the old generation's refusal. This is my reading; it overlaps with Dennis Olson's view of the daughters as models of the new generation's faith.

sections.b: Numbers 31 is presented as "the LORD's vengeance" on Midian for Peor. Twelve thousand men kill the men and kings of Midian and bring back women, children and spoil. Moses then orders every boy and every woman who has slept with a man killed, and the girls kept (31:14–18). The chapter goes on to purify the soldiers, because killing defiles even in a commanded war, and to divide the spoil. It is one of the hardest texts in the Bible. Defenders read it as a unique judgment on a people that tried to destroy Israel's faith; critical scholars read it as a late, idealized war story; many Jewish and Christian readers set it within the Bible's wider limits on war and call to mercy.

On the plains of Moab God commands Israel to drive out the inhabitants of Canaan and destroy their images and high places, warning that if Israel copies them, Israel too will be driven out (Numbers 33:50–56). The command is "drive out" rather than the ban of Deuteronomy, and the warning makes Israel subject to the same judgment.

Balaam's fourth oracle sees a ruler "not yet" and "not close by": "a star will march out of Jacob, and a scepter will rise from Israel" (Numbers 24:17). It probably first celebrated David, who conquered Moab and Edom (2 Samuel 8). The Greek translation turned the scepter into "a man" and the king of 24:7 into a man from Israel's seed who rules many nations. The Targums read "the Messiah will be anointed from Israel." The Dead Sea Scrolls applied the star and scepter to the coming Interpreter of the Law and Prince (CD 7:18–21). Rabbi Akiva applied it to Simon "Bar Kokhba," "son of the star," in AD 132, and Christians linked it with the star of the Magi (Matthew 2:2) and Jesus as "the bright Morning Star" (Revelation 22:16).
sections.refs: Numbers 24:7; Numbers 24:14–19; Genesis 49:10; 2 Samuel 8:2–14; Matthew 2:1–12; Revelation 22:16

uncommon: Some scholars think Balaam's star oracle originally referred only to David and became messianic only after the end of the Davidic kings.

sections.b: On the plains of Moab, after the plague at Peor, Moses and Eleazar count the new generation by clans: 601,730 men of twenty and up, and 23,000 Levites (Numbers 26). Not one man counted at Sinai is left except Caleb and Joshua (26:64–65), so the census proves God's oath fulfilled. It also sets the size of each tribe's land (26:52–56). Simeon falls most sharply, from 59,300 to 22,200, which many link with Peor.

Of the Levites' forty-eight cities, six are to be cities of refuge, three on each side of the Jordan, for Israelites and foreigners alike (Numbers 35:6, 11–15). The law gives tests for murder (an iron tool, a deadly stone or wooden object, hatred, ambush) and for accident (suddenly, without hostility, without seeing). The community judges between the killer and the avenger of blood. A murderer must die; one who killed by accident lives in the city until the high priest's death, and leaving it puts him at risk. No ransom may be taken for a murderer, and no one may die on one witness, because blood pollutes the land where God lives (35:30–34).

sections.h: The death of the high priest
sections.b: Why does the high priest's death free the refugee? The Talmud says it atones for the death (Bavli Makkot 11b) and tells that high priests' mothers brought food to refugees so they would not pray for their sons' deaths. Christian writers saw a picture of Christ, the high priest whose death frees the guilty, and of believers "who have fled for refuge" (Hebrews 6:18).

When Moses learns he will die, he asks God for a leader so the people will not be "like sheep with no one to shepherd them." God names Joshua, "a man who has the Spirit in him." Moses lays his hands on him before Eleazar and the community and gives him part of his honor; Joshua will learn God's will through Eleazar's Urim (Numbers 27:15–23). He and Eleazar will divide the land (34:17).

sections.h: Balak and the plains of Moab
sections.b: From Numbers 22 to the end of Deuteronomy, Israel camps on the plains of Moab. Balak, king of Moab, hires Balaam to curse Israel and hears four blessings instead, including a prophecy that a star from Jacob will "smash the brows of Moab" (Numbers 24:17). Then Moabite women draw Israel into the worship of the Baal of Peor (25:1–3). The Mesha stone shows that some towns of Numbers 32 (Ataroth, Dibon, Nebo) were still fought over by Moab and Israel around 840 BC.

Numbers 30 says a man's vow to the LORD must be kept. A young woman's vow in her father's house, or a wife's vow, binds her unless her father or husband cancels it on the day he hears; then "the LORD will forgive her." If he says nothing, it stands, and if he cancels it late, he bears her guilt. A widow's or divorced woman's vow stands like a man's (30:9). The rabbis built tractate Nedarim on this chapter and allowed sages to release rash vows, the background of Kol Nidre.

Numbers 28–29 lists the public offerings for every set time: two lambs daily, two more on the Sabbath, larger offerings at each new moon, at Passover and Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks, on the day of loud blasts, on the Day of Atonement, and above all at the Feast of Booths, with seventy bulls across its seven days and one more on the eighth. In a year it comes to 113 bulls and 1,093 lambs, besides rams and goats. Each offering is added "on top of the regular burnt offering," which is never skipped.

The tamid, a lamb each morning and evening with grain, oil and wine, is the base of Israel's worship (Numbers 28:3–8; Exodus 29:38–42). Its end under Antiochus IV is remembered in Daniel 8:11, and after AD 70 Jewish daily prayer took its place. Hebrews 10:11–14 contrasts the priests who stand "day after day" with Christ's single offering.

Israel's first great idolatry in the land of its future came at Peor: Moabite women invited the people to their gods' sacrifices, and Israel "tied itself to the Baal of Peor" (Numbers 25:1–3). Twenty-four thousand died. The memory runs through the Bible: Deuteronomy 4:3–4, Psalm 106:28–31, Hosea 9:10, and Paul's warning in 1 Corinthians 10:7–8.

Phinehas receives "a covenant of priesthood for all time" (Numbers 25:13), the claim on which the Zadokite high priests later rested (1 Chronicles 6:4–8). Eleazar now stands with Moses and Joshua at every key moment (26:1; 27:21; 31:12; 34:17). The Levites, with no tribal land, receive forty-eight cities with pastureland scattered among the tribes (35:1–8).

Numbers 34 draws the borders of Canaan before Israel crosses the Jordan: from the Wilderness of Zin and the Wadi of Egypt to Lebo-hamath, from the Great Sea to the Jordan. The land is to be divided by lot and by size (26:52–56; 33:54), and inheritance must stay within each tribe (36:7–9). Two and a half tribes settle east of the Jordan, outside these borders (32; 34:13–15).

sections.h: The tribes on the eve of the land
sections.b: The second census counts each tribe again (Numbers 26), with Simeon much reduced. Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh take land east of the Jordan on condition that their men fight alongside the rest (32). Each tribe names a chief to divide the land (34:16–29), listed roughly from south to north, as they would settle.

sections.h: Murder and the death penalty in Numbers 35
sections.b: Numbers 35 requires death for deliberate murder, carried out by the avenger of blood after the community has judged (35:16–21, 24). It forbids ransom for a murderer, so no one can buy off a life (35:31), and requires more than one witness (35:30). The rabbis kept the law in principle but set such strict standards of evidence that executions became extremely rare; the Mishnah calls a court that executes once in seven years "destructive" (Mishnah Makkot 1:10).

"Blood pollutes the land," and no atonement can be made for innocent blood except the blood of the one who shed it (Numbers 35:33). Like Abel's blood crying from the ground (Genesis 4:10), the shed blood of murder defiles the land where God lives (35:34).

Balak's elders bring "fees for divination" to Balaam (Numbers 22:7), and Joshua 13:22 calls him "the diviner." He goes off to seek omens at each altar (23:3, 15) until in 24:1 he stops. His second poem declares that "no omen works against Jacob" (23:23): Israel's God cannot be manipulated by magic.

The same word go'el names the "avenger of blood" in Numbers 35: the nearest relative who answers for a murdered kinsman. The cities of refuge limit him, so that no one dies before the community has judged (Numbers 35:12, 19–27).

Numbers 33:38–39 gives the only exact date of a death in the Torah: Aaron died on Mount Hor on the first day of the fifth month in the fortieth year, aged 123. Deuteronomy 10:6 places his death at Moserah, which may be a district near the mountain or a different tradition.

Numbers 29:12–38 sets the offerings for the seven days of the feast in the seventh month and the closing assembly on the eighth. The bulls go down by one each day, from thirteen to seven, seventy in all, far more than any other feast. The rabbis counted them as offerings for the seventy nations of the world (Genesis 10), so that Israel's feast prayed for all peoples; on the eighth day a single bull stands for Israel alone (Bavli Sukkah 55b). Zechariah 14:16–19 pictures the nations coming up to keep this feast.

Numbers 29:7–11 adds the public offerings for the tenth day of the seventh month: a holy gathering, no work at all, and the command "You are to humble yourselves," the words Leviticus 16:29–31 and 23:27–32 use. Besides the rites of Leviticus 16, the day has a bull, a ram, seven lambs and a goat as a sin offering. The same phrase "humble herself" in Numbers 30:13 shows that vows to fast were common, and that the Day of Atonement fast was the model.

In his last short oracles Balaam "saw Amalek" and said, "Amalek was first among the nations, / but his end will be destruction" (Numbers 24:20). Rashi and Ibn Ezra read "first" as the first nation to attack Israel after the exodus (Exodus 17:8–16). The third oracle had already named Agag, Amalek's king in Saul's day (Numbers 24:7; 1 Samuel 15), though the Greek reads Gog there.

sections.h: The sons of Korah did not die
sections.b: The second census recalls Korah's rebellion and adds, "But the sons of Korah did not die" (Numbers 26:9–11). Their line went on to serve in the temple: Heman the singer was a descendant of Korah (1 Chronicles 6:33–37), and eleven psalms (Psalms 42; 44–49; 84–85; 87–88) are headed "of the sons of Korah." The rabbis said Korah's sons turned back in their hearts at the last moment and a high place was set for them (Bavli Sanhedrin 110a).
